claims.text: Rapid quenching during synthesis produces a more uniformly mixed, single-phase noble metal–based HEA nanoparticle structure than slower cooling.
Rapidly quenched HEA nanoparticles have more evenly distributed active sites than slowly cooled nanoparticles.
The structural and active-site uniformity produced by rapid quenching enhances catalytic performance relative to slower cooling.
Slower cooling of conventionally processed HEA nanoparticles typically results in slight elemental inhomogeneity or segregation.
Rapid quenching kinetically freezes the alloy structure.
Thermal diffusion during cooling leads to elemental segregation in the relevant HEA nanoparticles.
Rapid quenching minimizes the thermal diffusion responsible for elemental segregation.
Suppressing segregation locks in a homogeneously mixed nanoparticle structure.
A homogeneously mixed structure promotes more consistent electronic distributions.
A homogeneously mixed structure increases the density of active sites needed for effective catalytic reactions.
Rapidly quenched nanoparticles will show a more uniform single-phase structure by TEM and XRD than the slowly cooled baseline.
Rapidly quenched nanoparticles will exhibit higher turnover frequency and conversion rates than the slowly cooled baseline.
Minor elemental segregation in slowly cooled nanoparticles reduces active-site uniformity and catalytic efficiency.
The proposed effect is expected to hold when thermal diffusion during synthesis is the dominant influence on elemental mixing in nanoscale noble metal–based HEAs.
The proposed effect may not apply to microscale materials or systems with significant surface oxidation.
The magnitude of the quenching-induced enhancement may depend on alloy composition, quenching rate, and subsequent surface conditions.
